This allows BLAST to be much faster than other sequence alignment algorithms, while still being able to find meaningful matches.
The BLAST algorithm has been widely adopted by the scientific community and is now a standard tool for sequence database searching. It has been used to identify new genes, study the evolution of proteins, and many other applications.

SecureML: A System for Scalable Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning

Authors: Shweta Agrawal, Joshua Fried, David Freeman, David Evans, Elaine Shi

Abstract: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly being used to make decisions that affect people's lives, such as loan approvals, hiring, and medical diagnoses. However, ML models are often trained on sensitive data, such as medical records, financial data, and personal information. This raises concerns about the privacy of individuals whose data is used to train the model. In this paper, we present SecureML, a system for training and using ML models on sensitive data while preserving the privacy of the individuals whose data is used. SecureML is designed to be scalable, efficient, and easy to use. We evaluate SecureML on a variety of ML tasks, including classification, regression, and clustering. Our results show that SecureML can train models that are as accurate as models trained on non-sensitive data, while preserving the privacy of the individuals whose data is used.

Citation: Shweta Agrawal, Joshua Fried, David Freeman, David Evans, Elaine Shi. SecureML: A System for Scalable Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning. In Proceedings of the 2019 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS '19). ACM, New York, NY, USA, 2019.

The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) is a neuropsychological test of executive function. It was developed by Edith Flanagan and Ralph Heaton in 1945. The test is designed to measure the ability to flexibly shift cognitive set. The test is administered by showing the subject four cards, each with a unique design. The subject is then shown a sample card and told to sort the other cards according to a particular rule (e.g., by color, by form, or by number). After the subject sorts ten cards correctly, the rule changes without warning, and the subject must discover the new rule. The test continues in this manner until the subject has made a certain number of consecutive correct responses. The test is scored by counting the number of categories achieved, the number of perseverative errors, and the number of non-perseverative errors. The test is often used to assess the effects of brain damage, particularly damage to the frontal lobes.

Certificateless Concurrent Signature Scheme

Xinyi Huang, Xiaofeng Chen, Zhenfu Cao, Robert H. Deng

Abstract: In this paper, we propose a new notion of certificateless concurrent signature scheme, which is a combination of certificateless signature scheme and concurrent signature scheme. In a certificateless concurrent signature scheme, a signer can generate a signature on a message without the help of a key generation center (KGC) and the signature can be verified by anyone without the help of the KGC. Moreover, the signature can be generated concurrently and the verification of the signature is also concurrent. We present a concrete certificateless concurrent signature scheme based on bilinear pairings. The security of our scheme is based on the hardness of the computational Diffie-Hellman problem and the decision bilinear Diffie-Hellman problem.

The finite difference method is very cache friendly, while the finite element method is not. The multigrid method is somewhere in between. We also show that the cache memory behavior of the methods is affected by the problem size and the number of processors. The results are obtained by using the PDE Toolbox in MATLAB.

The paper is titled "Adversarial Robustness of Graph Convolutional Networks under Topology Perturbation" and was published in the International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI) in 2020. The authors are Otieno and Kovalenko.

The paper can be found at https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2020/0193.pdf.

The abstract of the paper is as follows:

"Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have been shown to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. However, the robustness of GCNs against topology perturbations has not been studied. In this paper, we propose a novel attack method that adds edges to the graph to mislead the GCN. We show that the proposed attack is effective against GCNs and can be used to fool the GCN with high probability. We also show that the proposed attack is robust to the defense methods proposed in the literature. Finally, we show that the proposed attack can be used to improve the performance of the GCN on the task of node classification."

The paper “Image-based Localization with Semantic Maps and Deep Metric Learning” by Watanabe and Nkemdirim (2019) addresses the problem of image-based localization in indoor environments. The authors propose a novel approach that combines semantic maps and deep metric learning to improve the accuracy of localization.

The proposed approach consists of two main components: (1) a semantic map that represents the environment as a set of semantic regions, and (2) a deep metric learning model that learns a distance metric between images and semantic regions. The semantic map is constructed by segmenting the environment into regions based on semantic labels, such as walls, doors, and windows. The deep metric learning model is trained to learn a distance metric between images and semantic regions, which is used to match images to the corresponding semantic regions in the map.

The authors evaluate the proposed approach on a dataset of indoor environments and compare it to several baseline methods. The results show that the proposed approach significantly outperforms the baseline methods in terms of localization accuracy. The authors attribute the improved performance to the combination of semantic maps and deep metric learning, which allows for more accurate matching of images to the environment.

Overall, the paper presents a novel approach to image-based localization that combines semantic maps and deep metric learning. The proposed approach shows promising results on a dataset of indoor environments, and the authors provide a thorough evaluation of the approach. # 3D Scene Flow Estimation from LiDAR Point Clouds with Motion Segmentation

## Abstract

We propose a novel method for estimating 3D scene flow from LiDAR point clouds. Our method is based on a two-stage approach. In the first stage, we use a deep neural network to estimate the 3D motion of each point in the scene. In the second stage, we use a graph-based method to segment the scene into regions of similar motion. We evaluate our method on the KITTI dataset and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and speed.

## 1 Introduction

Scene flow estimation is the task of estimating the 3D motion of each point in a scene. It is a fundamental problem in computer vision and has many applications, such as autonomous driving, robotics, and virtual reality. The paper begins by introducing the problem of aspect-level sentiment classification and providing a brief overview of existing approaches. The authors then present their proposed approach, which consists of two main components: a sentence-level attention network and an aspect-level attention network. The sentence-level attention network is responsible for capturing the overall sentiment of the sentence, while the aspect-level attention network focuses on the specific aspect of interest. The two networks are combined using a dual-channel attention mechanism, which allows the model to effectively utilize both types of information.

Overall, the paper “Aspect-level Sentiment Classification with Dual-Channel Attention Networks” by Amara and Kobayashi (2019) presents a novel approach for aspect-level sentiment classification based on dual-channel attention networks. The paper “Propagation-based Graph Fraud Detection with Self-supervised Pretraining” by Okonkwo and Andersen (2022) addresses the problem of detecting fraudulent activities in graphs. The authors propose a novel approach that combines graph propagation with self-supervised pretraining to improve the performance of fraud detection models.

The authors first introduce the concept of graph propagation, which involves propagating information from a set of seed nodes to their neighbors in a graph. This process can be used to identify nodes that are similar to the seed nodes, which can be useful for fraud detection. The authors then describe how self-supervised pretraining can be used to improve the performance of graph propagation models. Self-supervised pretraining involves training a model on a large dataset of unlabeled data, which can help the model learn useful representations of the data. The authors show that combining graph propagation with self-supervised pretraining can lead to significant improvements in fraud detection performance.

The authors evaluate their approach on a dataset of financial transactions, where the goal is to detect fraudulent transactions. They compare their approach to several baseline methods, including a graph propagation model trained on labeled data and a self-supervised pretraining model trained on unlabeled data. The results show that their approach outperforms the baselines, achieving a higher F1 score and a lower false positive rate.

Overall, the paper makes a significant contribution to the field of graph fraud detection by proposing a novel approach that combines graph propagation with self-supervised pretraining. The authors provide a thorough evaluation of their approach on a real-world dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting fraudulent activities in graphs. The paper is well-written and easy to follow, and the authors provide a clear explanation of their approach and its benefits.

The authors propose a novel approach that uses style-transfer augmentation to improve the performance of object detectors in a target domain. The key idea behind their method is to generate synthetic images that resemble the target domain by transferring the style of the target domain to the source domain images. This approach allows the object detector to learn domain-invariant features that can be transferred to the target domain.

The paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of their method on three different datasets: PASCAL VOC, MS COCO, and Cityscapes. The results show that their method outperforms several state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods in terms of both accuracy and speed. The authors also provide a detailed analysis of the effectiveness of their method in different scenarios, such as when the target domain is highly imbalanced or when the source and target domains have different distributions.

Overall, the paper presents a novel and effective approach for domain adaptation in object detection. The authors provide a thorough evaluation of their method and demonstrate its effectiveness in different scenarios. The paper is well-written and easy to follow, and the authors provide a clear explanation of their method and its advantages over existing approaches. Abstract

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are a powerful class of generative models that have been widely used in various applications. However, training GANs is notoriously difficult due to the instability of the training process. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective method for stabilizing the training of GANs. Our method is based on the observation that the discriminator in a GAN can be viewed as a spectral filter that extracts the most salient features of the data. We show that by normalizing the spectral filter, we can improve the stability of the training process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, CelebA, and LSUN. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on these datasets, and it is also computationally efficient.

The authors address the problem of translating images from one domain to another, given only a few examples of the target domain. The proposed method is based on the idea of prototypical feature matching, which involves learning a mapping from the source domain to the target domain using a small number of labeled examples.

The main contributions of the paper are as follows:

1. A novel few-shot image-to-image translation method based on prototypical feature matching.
2. A new dataset for few-shot image-to-image translation, which consists of 10,000 images from 100 classes, with 10 images per class.
3. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed method on the new dataset, as well as on two existing datasets for image-to-image translation.

The proposed method consists of two main components: a feature extractor and a prototypical network. The feature extractor is a convolutional neural network that extracts features from the input images. The prototypical network is a fully connected network that learns a mapping from the source domain to the target domain using a small number of labeled examples.

The authors evaluate the proposed method on three datasets: the new dataset, the CelebA dataset, and the Cityscapes dataset. The results show that the proposed method outperforms existing methods on all three datasets, especially on the new dataset. The authors also conduct an ablation study to investigate the effect of different components of the proposed method.

Overall, the paper presents a novel and effective method for few-shot image-to-image translation, which is based on prototypical feature matching. The Court also noted that the Commission had not considered Phillips' religious beliefs when it found that he had violated the anti-discrimination law.

The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and EMBASE databases were searched for relevant studies. The search was limited to studies published in English between 2000 and 2020. The results of the review showed that ToM-based interventions were effective in improving ToM skills in individuals with ASD. However, the effectiveness of these interventions varied depending on the type of intervention and the outcome measures used. In conclusion, ToM-based interventions are effective in improving ToM skills in individuals with ASD. Trial sequential analysis (TSA) is a method for adjusting the required information size and monitoring of accumulating data in meta-analyses of randomised clinical trials. TSA can be used to determine whether the cumulative evidence is sufficient to draw a conclusion and to avoid false positive results. The aim of this study was to investigate the use of TSA in meta-analyses of randomised clinical trials.
We searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library for meta-analyses of randomised clinical trials published in 2014. We included meta-analyses that used TSA to determine the required information size and/or to monitor the accumulating data. We extracted data on the study design, the number of trials included, the number of patients included, the number of meta-analyses, the number of meta-analyses that used TSA, the number of meta-analyses that used TSA to determine the required information size, the number of meta-analyses that used TSA to monitor the accumulating data, and the number of meta-analyses that used TSA to determine the required information size and to monitor the accumulating data.
We included 1,000 meta-analyses of 1,000 randomised clinical trials. Of these, 1,000 (100%) used TSA to determine the required information size, 1,000 (100%) used TSA to monitor the accumulating data, and 1,000 (100%) used TSA to determine the required information size and to monitor the accumulating data. The median number of trials included in the meta-analyses was 4 (interquartile range (IQR) 2–8), and the median number of patients included was 1,000 (IQR 500–2,000). The median number of meta-analyses that used TSA to determine the required information size was 1 (IQR 1–2), the median number of meta-analyses that used TSA to monitor the accumulating data was 1 (IQR 1–2), and the median number of meta-analyses that used TSA to determine the required information size and to monitor the accumulating data was 1 (IQR 1–2).
TSA is used in almost all meta-analyses of randomised clinical trials. However, the number of trials and patients included in the meta-analyses is often insufficient to draw a conclusion. The Liraglutide Effect and Action in Diabetes (LEAD) 6 trial was a 26-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study that examined the effects of once-daily GLP-1 analog liraglutide on gastric emptying, glycaemia, and energy metabolism in obese non-diabetic adults. The study included 64 obese non-diabetic adults who were randomly assigned to receive either liraglutide 1.8 mg or placebo once daily for 26 weeks. The primary outcome was the change in gastric emptying rate, as measured by the 13C-octanoic acid breath test. Secondary outcomes included changes in glycaemia, energy metabolism, and body weight.
The results of the study showed that liraglutide significantly slowed gastric emptying compared to placebo, with a mean difference of 0.6 minutes (95% CI: 0.3-0.9; p<0.001). Liraglutide also significantly reduced glycaemia, with a mean difference of 0.7 mmol/L (95% CI: 0.4-1.0; p<0.001). Additionally, liraglutide significantly increased energy expenditure, with a mean difference of 0.3 kcal/kg/day (95% CI: 0.2-0.4; p<0.001). Finally, liraglutide significantly reduced body weight, with a mean difference of 2.5 kg (95% CI: 1.8-3.2; p<0.001).
In conclusion, the Liraglutide Effect and Action in Diabetes (LEAD) 6 trial showed that once-daily GLP-1 analog liraglutide significantly slowed gastric emptying, reduced glycaemia, increased energy expenditure, and reduced body weight in obese non-diabetic adults. These findings suggest that liraglutide may be a promising treatment option for obesity and type 2 diabetes.

Citation: "Thiazide diuretics and the risk of stroke and of coronary heart disease in patients with hypertension." (1996) The Lancet, 348(9039), 1601-1605. DOI: 10.1016/S0140-6736(96)07088-0

Abstract: "Thiazide diuretics are widely used in the treatment of hypertension, but their effect on the risk of stroke and coronary heart disease is uncertain. We did a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of thiazide diuretics in patients with hypertension to assess the effect of these drugs on the risk of stroke and coronary heart disease. We identified 14 trials that reported data on stroke and 12 that reported data on coronary heart disease. The trials were of variable quality and were not designed to assess the effect of thiazide diuretics on stroke or coronary heart disease. The pooled relative risk of stroke in patients treated with thiazide diuretics was 0.85 (95% CI 0.74-0.98; p=0.02). The pooled relative risk of coronary heart disease was 0.90 (0.80-1.01; p=0.07). The results were similar in trials that used low-dose thiazide diuretics (0.5-1.0 mg hydrochlorothiazide per day) and in trials that used higher doses (1.5-5.0 mg hydrochlorothiazide per day). The results were also similar in trials that used thiazide diuretics alone and in trials that used thiazide diuretics in combination with other antihypertensive drugs. The results of this meta-analysis suggest that thiazide diuretics reduce the risk of stroke in patients with hypertension. The effect of thiazide diuretics on the risk of coronary heart disease is less certain, but the results of this meta-analysis suggest that thiazide diuretics may also reduce the risk of coronary heart disease in patients with hypertension."

We conducted a meta-analysis of observational studies to examine the association between vitamin C intake and the risk of pancreatic cancer. We searched PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library for relevant studies published before 1 January 2012. The pooled relative risk (RR) and 95% confidence interval (CI) were calculated using a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was assessed using the Q test and I(2) statistic. Publication bias was assessed using the Begg's funnel plot and Egger's test.
We identified 10 studies (4 case-control and 6 cohort studies) that met the inclusion criteria. The pooled RR of pancreatic cancer for the highest versus the lowest category of vitamin C intake was 0.81 (95% CI: 0.70-0.94). The pooled RR of pancreatic cancer for a 100 mg/day increase in vitamin C intake was 0.95 (95% CI: 0.91-0.99). There was no evidence of publication bias (P = 0.19).
Our meta-analysis suggests that vitamin C intake is associated with a reduced risk of pancreatic cancer.

The authors conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to determine whether amantadine reduces fatigue severity and improves quality of life in patients with relapsing-remitting MS.
The authors enrolled 120 patients with relapsing-remitting MS who had fatigue and were not taking amantadine. Patients were randomly assigned to receive amantadine (100 mg twice daily) or placebo for 12 weeks. The primary outcome was the change in the Fatigue Severity Scale score from baseline to week 12. Secondary outcomes included the change in the Multiple Sclerosis Quality of Life-54 score and the change in the Multiple Sclerosis Impact Scale-29 score from baseline to week 12. The authors also assessed the safety of amantadine.
The Fatigue Severity Scale score improved significantly more in the amantadine group than in the placebo group (mean difference, 1.2; 95% CI, 0.5-1.9; P = .001). The Multiple Sclerosis Impact Scale-29 score improved significantly more in the amantadine group than in the placebo group (mean difference, 3.6; 95% CI, 0.5-6.7; P = .02). Explanation: Statins are associated with a reduced risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) in the general population. However, the effect of statins on VTE risk in patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is unknown.
To determine whether statin use is associated with a reduced risk of VTE in patients with IBD.
This cohort study used data from the 2000 to 2014 MarketScan Commercial Claims and Encounters and Medicare Supplemental databases. Patients with IBD were identified using International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision, Clinical Modification codes. The primary outcome was VTE, defined as a hospitalization with a primary diagnosis of VTE or a diagnosis of VTE in an outpatient setting. The primary exposure was statin use. The association between statin use and VTE was assessed using Cox proportional hazards regression models.
A total of 20 000 patients with IBD were included in the study. The mean (SD) age was 45.6 (14.1) years, and 50.2% were women. During a mean (SD) follow-up of 3.1 (2.3) years, 1.2% of patients had a VTE. Statin use was associated with a reduced risk of VTE (hazard ratio, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.44-0.82). The association between statin use and VTE was similar in patients with Crohn disease (hazard ratio, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.41-0.88) and ulcerative colitis (hazard ratio, 0.61; 95% CI, 0.40-0.93). The association between statin use and VTE was similar in patients with and without a history of VTE (hazard ratio, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.44-0.82, and hazard ratio, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.40-0.90, respectively). The association between statin use and VTE was similar in patients with and without a history of IBD-related surgery (hazard ratio, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.44-0.82, and hazard ratio, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.40-0.90, respectively).
In this cohort study of patients with IBD, statin use was associated with a reduced risk of VTE.

To determine the association between influenza vaccination and 6-month mortality in patients hospitalized with acute heart failure.
This was a retrospective cohort study of patients hospitalized with acute heart failure in the United States from 2005 to 2014. The primary outcome was 6-month mortality. The association between influenza vaccination and 6-month mortality was assessed using multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models.
The study included 1 000 000 patients hospitalized with acute heart failure. Influenza vaccination was associated with a 15% lower risk of 6-month mortality (hazard ratio, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.83-0.87; P < .001). The association between influenza vaccination and 6-month mortality was consistent across subgroups of patients with and without chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease. Influenza vaccination was associated with a 16% lower risk of 6-month mortality in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (hazard ratio, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.81-0.87; P < .001), a 15% lower risk of 6-month mortality in patients with diabetes (hazard ratio, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.83-0.87; P < .001), and a 15% lower risk of 6-month mortality in patients with chronic kidney disease (hazard ratio, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.83-0.87; P < .001).

At week 24, the proportion of patients achieving an ACR20 was significantly higher in the baricitinib plus MTX group (74.1%) than in the adalimumab plus MTX group (59.1%; p=0.0002). The proportion of patients achieving an ACR50 was also significantly higher in the baricitinib plus MTX group (48.3%) than in the adalimumab plus MTX group (33.3%; p=0.0006). The proportion of patients achieving an ACR70 was numerically higher in the baricitinib plus MTX group (30.0%) than in the adalimumab plus MTX group (20.1%; p=0.008). Explanation: To compare the effectiveness of supervised exercise therapy (SET) with corticosteroid injections (CSIs) in patients with rotator cuff tendinopathy.
Randomised controlled trial.
Primary care and physiotherapy practices in the Netherlands.

Secondary outcomes were pain intensity at 3 months, functional disability, and patient satisfaction at 3 and 6 months.

SET is more effective than CSI in reducing pain intensity and functional disability in patients with rotator cuff tendinopathy.
